evidence.label: The unique threshold bound state of the SU(N) BFSS model
Positive eigenvalues of the relative SU(2) BFSS Hamiltonian

headline: Claims the BFSS matrix model has exactly one zero-energy bound state for every N, and many positive-energy ones at N = 2.
scope: Undeformed SU(N) BFSS supersymmetric matrix quantum mechanics with the centre of mass removed, for every finite N ≥ 2.
plain: The BFSS model is a quantum system of nine large matrices and their fermion partners, proposed as a description of M-theory. Witten predicted that, for every matrix size N, it has exactly one trapped state of zero energy. Physics arguments supported this, but they relied on assumptions about far-away regions. One paper claims to prove the prediction for every N, and a second claims infinitely many trapped positive-energy states at N = 2. There is no Lean check.
doesNot: This does not prove the BFSS matrix-theory conjecture itself, or anything about the large-N limit.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Edward Witten, prediction of a unique D0-brane threshold bound state
scorecard.significanceWhy: The threshold-bound-state conjecture is a central assumption of the BFSS matrix-theory proposal in string theory.

explanation:
Take two vectors x¹ and x² in a plane, and use the energy V = |x¹ ∧ x²|². This is the squared area of the parallelogram they span. Put x¹ = (r, 0) and x² = (0, s). Then V = r²s². At r = 10 and s = 0.1, V = 1. If the vectors point the same way, V = 0 however long they are. So the energy has flat valleys running off to infinity. A classical ball can roll out along such a valley. A quantum particle might not, because the valley gets narrower as r grows.

The BFSS model uses a potential of this kind. It has nine Hermitian matrices, plus fermion partners, linked by supersymmetry. Supersymmetric matrix quantum mechanics first appeared in the study of supermembranes[1]. With SU(N) matrices it has 9(N² − 1) position coordinates. That is 27 for N = 2 and 72 for N = 3. Witten predicted that, with the centre of mass removed, every N has exactly one normalizable zero-energy state[2]. Normalizable means the wave stays concentrated, so the particles stay bound. In matrix theory, this state is the inner state of a single supergraviton carrying N units of momentum[3].

The state is hard to see because it sits at a threshold. The continuous spectrum, the energies of states that escape, starts at zero[4]. So the bound state has the same energy as states flying apart. Physicists counted zero-energy states with a supersymmetric index. In this noncompact problem, contributions from infinity are essential[5]. Sethi and Stern obtained the N = 2 index by including such a boundary term[6]. A general-N argument by Konechny assumed that certain matrix differences all grow at the same rate[7]. Controlling the regions where they do not is the main obstacle.

The first paper claims the full result. For every N ≥ 2, the model has exactly one normalizable zero-energy state after removing the centre of mass[8]. The paper calls this a proof of the threshold-bound-state conjecture.

The second paper looks at N = 2 above zero energy. The flat valleys appear when the three vectors in the model line up[9]. The paper claims an unbounded sequence of positive energies with trapped wave functions[10]. In some symmetry sectors, oscillation across the valley costs enough energy to hold the state in. The paper says this refutes, at N = 2, the original BFSS paper's exclusion of such states[11].

How sure is this? There is no Lean formalization for these papers. The claims rest on two papers, one of them long. No specialist review of them has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. There is no Lean check. Both the unique bound state and the N = 2 positive-energy states rest on two papers with no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: Banks–Fischler–Shenker–Susskind matrix quantum mechanics: nine Hermitian matrices and fermions, proposed as a description of M-theory.
A symmetry pairing boson and fermion degrees of freedom; here it makes zero the lowest possible energy.
A wave function with finite total probability, so the system stays bound rather than flying apart.
A bound state whose energy equals the lowest energy of escaping states, here zero.
The range of energies of states that are not bound, such as particles moving apart.
A count of zero-energy states, bosonic minus fermionic, used by physicists to predict bound states.
The group of N × N unitary matrices with determinant one; it sets the matrix size of the model.
